chapter.title: Putting out the last fire: Japan, and why the Allies won

cards.body:
The last house still burning is Japan, at the far end of the street across the water. By summer 1945 every hose on the street is pointed at it: American ships ring the islands, bombers come most nights, and in one August week the Soviet neighbour runs up with a hose of his own.

**The war ends the way it was won: by weight, not by one clever stroke.**

cards.prompt: August 1945. Japan's navy is mostly on the seabed, no oil tankers get through, cities burn nightly, the Soviet Union has just declared war, and two atomic bombs have fallen. Someone at the pub asks: 'So which one thing made Japan quit?' Your best answer?

options.text: The atomic bombs. Nothing else counted.
The Soviet attack. The bombs were a sideshow.
Trick question. It all landed in the same week, and Japan's leaders saw no way out in any direction.

whyNot.a: That's the most famous blow, not the only one: in the same week Japan's leaders also faced a Soviet army and a sea blockade that was starving the cities.
whyNot.b: That's one hose, not all of them: the Soviet attack mattered, but it arrived on top of two bombs and a blockade.

cards.reteach: Think of the fire. By August 1945 Japan was being hit from the sea, the air and, suddenly, the north. Historians still argue about which blow weighed most, but they agree it was the pile, not one brick.

cards.title: Island by island
cards.body:
After Midway in June 1942, the Americans fought across the Pacific one island at a time: Guadalcanal from August 1942, Saipan in July 1944, Iwo Jima and Okinawa in the first half of 1945. Each was a step closer, and each cost thousands of lives on both sides.

Why islands? Each one captured was an airfield nearer Japan. From Saipan and its neighbours, B-29 bombers could reach Tokyo. American submarines sank the tankers bringing oil from the south.

**By summer 1945 Japan could not fuel its planes or feed its cities, and its army still refused to quit.** An invasion of Japan itself was planned for November.

cards.title: One week in August
cards.body:
6 August 1945: an American plane drops an *atomic bomb*, a single bomb with the force of thousands of ordinary ones, on Hiroshima. 8 August: the Soviet Union declares war on Japan, and the next morning its tanks roll into Manchuria, the part of China Japan held. 9 August: a second bomb hits Nagasaki.

Japan's leaders had been hoping Moscow would help them bargain for softer terms. That hope and two cities died in the same four days. On 15 August the Emperor spoke on the radio, the first time most Japanese had ever heard his voice, to say the war was over. **The papers were signed on 2 September 1945**, on the battleship Missouri in Tokyo Bay: six years and one day after Poland.

cards.prompt: Your cousin is writing a school essay titled 'The bomb that ended the war'. Which change makes the essay match what actually happened in August 1945?

options.text: Keep the title. Hiroshima on 6 August ended the war that same day.
Retitle it 'The week that ended the war': two bombs, a Soviet invasion and a blockade, all between 6 and 9 August.
Retitle it 'The Soviet army that ended the war'. The bombs barely mattered.

whyNot.a: That's the first blow, not the end: Japan did not surrender on 6 August. The Emperor spoke on 15 August, after Nagasaki and the Soviet attack.
whyNot.c: That's swinging too far the other way: the Soviet attack was one hose among several, not the only one.

cards.reteach: Hiroshima alone did not do it, and neither did Moscow alone. Between 6 and 9 August Japan lost two cities, its last hope of a Soviet go-between, and any chance of feeding itself by sea. The surrender followed that pile-up, not any single piece of it.

cards.title: Four reasons the Allies won
cards.body:
Now step back and look at the whole street. **Four things, each from a chapter you've read.**

*Numbers.* From December 1941 Germany and Japan were fighting Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States at once (chapter 4). Those three together had more people, oil and steel than the Axis by a wide margin.

*Factories.* America built ships and planes faster than the Axis could sink or shoot them down, and Soviet factories moved east, out of reach (chapter 6).

*Sea lanes.* Atlantic convoys got through, and Midway sank Japan's carriers (chapter 5).

*Teamwork.* The Allies planned together. Germany and Japan fought separate wars: Japan never attacked the Soviet Union, so Stalin could throw everything at Germany (chapter 4).

At a pub quiz, Dev hears 'why did the Allies win?' and says 'the atom bomb', then stops. Spot the slip with one question: which side had more steel, oil, ships and soldiers in 1944? If the answer is the Allies by a mile, the bomb cannot be the whole story. **It ended the war. It did not win it.** Germany had already surrendered three months before Hiroshima.

cards.prompt: Four reasons the Allies won. Which list holds up against the chapters you've read?

options.text: Braver soldiers, better generals, luck at Midway, the atomic bomb.
More people and oil, more factory output, sea lanes kept open, and Allies who planned together while the Axis fought separate wars.
Munich, the fall of France, Pearl Harbor, D-Day.

whyNot.a: That's a list of feelings and moments, not weights: brave soldiers fought on both sides, and the bomb came after Germany had already surrendered.
whyNot.c: Those are turning points from chapters 2 to 6, not reasons: they tell you when the fire spread or turned, not why one side had more water.

cards.reteach: Ask of each reason: did it give one side more water on the fire, month after month? More people, more factories, open supply lines and a shared plan all do. A single battle or a single bomb does not, however dramatic.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Japan was squeezed island by island until, in one August week of 1945, two atomic bombs and a Soviet invasion left its leaders no way out, and the surrender was signed on 2 September. **The Allies won because they had more people, more factories, open sea lanes and a shared plan**, not because of one bomb or one battle.

Tonight, tell someone the whole war in 10 minutes: 1919, Munich, Poland, France, 1941, the three turning battles, D-Day, Berlin, August 1945. Count the turning points on your fingers. Wherever you stall is tomorrow's reread.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain how the war with Japan ended in August 1945 and give four concrete reasons the Allies won, each tied to a chapter you have read.
